# Vault 112

## Overview

Vault 112 is a fictional research and containment facility within Bethesda Softworks’ Fallout video game series, most prominently featured in Fallout 3. Unlike most vaults in the post-apocalyptic Fallout universe, Vault 112 was designed for experimental virtual reality confinement rather than traditional survival. Its small population was maintained in a perpetual state of suspended animation via advanced simulation technology. The vault’s location, narrative significance, and the dark ethical themes explored in its associated quest “Tranquility Lane” have made it a subject of ongoing discussion among players, critics, and scholars .

## Origins and Context

Vault 112 was one of many vaults constructed by the Vault-Tec Corporation supposedly as a means to ensure humanity’s survival in the event of nuclear war. However, as with other facilities, its underlying purpose was to serve as a controlled environment for social experimentation. Vault 112 is located beneath Smith Casey’s garage in the Capital Wasteland—an area based on the ruins of northern Virginia in Fallout 3’s setting. The vault differs from others in that it holds only 85 inhabitants, each confined to an individual “Tranquility Lounger”—a pod designed to keep its occupant sedated and fully immersed in a shared virtual reality .

## Purpose and Experimental Design

The stated purpose of Vault 112 was to observe the long-term psychological effects of permanent virtual reality confinement. Overseen by the scientist Dr. Stanislaus Braun, the experiment’s stated goals were concealed from most residents. Dr. Braun used his access privileges to manipulate every aspect of the simulation, effectively making himself an omnipotent figure within the facility’s digital world. Over time, he used this control to subject the vault’s occupants to a variety of psychological traumas, often for his own amusement . The design and operation of Vault 112 highlight recurring themes in the Fallout series: unchecked scientific authority, ethical boundaries in experimentation, and the nature of reality .

## Notable Features

Vault 112 is characterized by several distinctive technological and narrative elements:

- **Tranquility Loungers**: These are the signature devices of Vault 112. Resembling advanced stasis pods, each Lounger connects the user’s mind to the communal simulation, maintaining both physical stasis and neural immersion.
- **Automation**: The entire vault is operated with minimal human oversight, as residents remain unconscious and sedated while the automated systems handle life support and security.
- **The Tranquility Lane Simulation**: The simulation, designed by Dr. Braun, recreates an idyllic 1950s American suburb. This setting becomes the principal site of interaction for both residents and the player-character in Fallout 3. While superficially cheerful, Tranquility Lane is the setting for psychological torment inflicted upon the residents at Braun’s direction .
- **Control and Manipulation**: Dr. Braun retains administrative control, allowing him to alter events, personalities, and outcomes in real time, frequently subjecting residents to scenarios involving distress, violence, or moral dilemmas .

## Role and Depiction in Fallout 3

Vault 112 is central to a main-quest sequence in Fallout 3. The player enters the vault while searching for their missing father, discovering both the physical facility and the simulated Tranquility Lane. Within the simulation, the player must navigate a series of disturbing moral challenges set by Dr. Braun, ultimately finding a way to free themselves and their father from virtual captivity . The representation of Vault 112 and its storyline are often cited as an example of the franchise's capacity to combine black comedy, horror, and social commentary .

## Reception and Critical Analysis

Vault 112’s “Tranquility Lane” quest is widely recognized as one of Fallout 3’s most memorable and discussed narrative sequences. Critics have frequently praised its unsettling atmosphere, innovative use of simulation, and the way it prompts players to confront ethical dilemmas and the consequences of unchecked authority . Academic analysis has noted the scenario’s effective use of role reversal and player agency, as well as its broader reflections on dystopian control and the loss of autonomy . The character of Dr. Braun, in particular, has been identified as a powerful representation of scientific hubris and moral detachment .

## Controversies and Thematic Debates

Vault 112 has provoked notable debate among critics and players regarding its themes and the depiction of psychological experimentation and simulated suffering. The storyline raises questions about technology’s potential for abuse, issues of free will, and the ethics of experimental science as depicted in entertainment media . While most analysis focuses on the quality of storytelling and player engagement, some discussions also touch on broader questions of morality in video game narratives.

## Cultural Impact and Legacy

Vault 112’s influence is largely confined to the Fallout franchise and its related fan and critical communities. The vault has not appeared as a significant reference outside the series but remains a touchstone within retrospectives, reviews, and academic studies concerned with video game narrative design and the ethical use of simulation .

## Appearances in Other Media

Vault 112 is primarily featured in Fallout 3 and related official guidebooks and has not appeared in significant form outside this context. Its “Tranquility Lane” sequence is occasionally referenced in critical essays, game retrospectives, and academic works focusing on virtual reality and dystopian fiction within gaming .

## See Also

- Dr. Stanislaus Braun
- Tranquility Lane

[Bloodborne](https://www.gamespot.com/bloodborne/) is coming out exclusively for the PlayStation 4, but many fans of developer From Software's previous games, [Dark Souls](https://www.gamespot.com/dark-souls/) and [Dark Souls 2](https://www.gamespot.com/dark-souls-ii/), were able to play them on [PC](https://www.gamespot.com/pc/) and [Xbox 360](https://www.gamespot.com/xbox-360/) in addition to the [PlayStation 3](https://www.gamespot.com/ps3/).

According to the game's director Hidetaka Miyazaki, Bloodborne couldn't have come out on previous consoles. "I always wanted to make a game set in the Victorian era, but to make it look good—with all the clothing and the architecture and things—required a console more powerful than the ones that were around. the arrival of the PS4 finally gave us that," Miyazaki said in an interview with [PlayStation LifeStyle](http://www.playstationlifestyle.net/2014/09/26/bloodborne-director-explains-game-ps4-exclusive-says-possible-ps4/#/slide/1) when asked why the game was a PS4-exclusive. "Bloodborne isn’t a game that could have been cross-generation, it was only possible on PS4."

Of course, that doesn't really explain why it's not coming out on Xbox One or PC, but that probably has more to do with Sony's negotiating skills than technological limitations.

Bloodborne will be released on [February 6](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/bloodborne-release-date-confirmed-new-trailer-goes/1100-6422394/) in North America and Europe, a day after it's release in Japan.
